newsitem.title: USA: IMF defends debt initiative, sees more in pipeline.
newsitem.headline: IMF defends debt initiative, sees more in pipeline.

text.p: The IMF, facing charges a debt write-off plan for poor nations is going too slowly, said on Sunday another five or six countries will be lined up to benefit from the initiative in the next few months.

IMF official Jack Boorman said that in addition to debt relief already promised to Uganda, decisions were due on Bolivia, Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast shortly, while another two or three nations would be considered in the coming months.
He cited Guyana and Mozambique as likely "to be on the agenda reasonably quickly".
He also said that the initiative, which in Africa has been overshadowed by civil war in Zaire, was only a small part of attempts to help the world's poorest nations.
"They are faced with numerous problems and debt is one of them and this initiative is aimed at that particular problem. It is a piece of a very large pie," he said.
He said the International Monetary Fund would look closely at military spending in countries likely to benefit to make sure money from debt relief was not diverted to arms.
"We will also be looking at military spending. We have tried to bring greater attention to this in all countries. We will continue to do so," he said.

Concern about an increase in military spending by Uganda, alleged to be helping rebels fighting to oust President Mobutu Sese Seko in Zaire, had been a sticking point in talks on giving it debt relief, officials have said.

World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Friday Uganda had been warned about military spending and said he had received assurances money from the debt relief, meant to go to schools, hospitals and other social purposes, would not be diverted.
The IMF and World Bank approved the debt relief for Uganda last week, making it the first to benefit from the initiative, which is being carried out jointly with the Paris Club of creditor nations.
Around 15 to 20 countries, mostly in Africa, are expected to benefit, at a total cost to their creditors estimated at between $5.5 billion and $8.4 billion.

The initiative, however, has been criticized by aid agencies who say the procedures for approving and providing debt relief are too slow -- Uganda will not get its relief of around $340 million until April 1998.

"Discussions on the first countries...have fuelled fears that the vast majority of poor indebted countries in need of immediate debt relief will only receive this beyond the year 2000," development watchdog Eurodad said in a statement.
"The amount of money at stake for creditors does not justify the continued existence of millions of people in abject poverty," it added.
Developing countries said on Saturday they wanted a more flexible interpretation of the initiative to allow more countries to benefit and more resources pumped into the plan.
But Boorman, director of the IMF's policy development and review department, said the procedures were necessary to ensure a fair assessment of a country's right to qualify for debt relief.

"Clearly we have not pleased everybody. Some have complained the relief is too little, some powerful voices have said exactly the opposite," he said, noting that rich countries faced tough budget contraints at home, limiting help for poor nations.
He noted the IMF and World Bank had agreed to broaden criteria for qualifying for the debt relief to allow countries with open economies and strong exports to benefit.
These would previously have been excluded by a requirement that debt service charges be 200 to 250 percent of export revenues.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said on Saturday these broader guidelines should allow Ivory Coast, Guyana, Yemen, Congo and Mauritania to benefit.
